<div class="sheet">

  <div class="ws-head">
    <div>
      <h1>Regulatory Scope and Required Posture Matrix</h1>
      <p class="ws-sub">A signed statement of regulatory scope and the governance capabilities that are non-negotiable for this organization.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="ws-meta">
      <b>WS-05-compliance-scope-and-posture-matrix</b><br>
      Pack E - Guardrails: authority, risk and proof<br>
      fill order <b>2</b> &middot; type <b>matrix</b><br>
      audience <b>exec</b>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="ws-source">
    Source: <b>Governance for AI-Assisted Delivery</b>, <i>Compliance Framework Mapping</i> &middot;
    <code>handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.qmd</code> L75-96 &middot;
    <a href="https://danielmeppiel.github.io/agentic-sdlc-handbook/handbook/ch05-governance-for-ai-assisted-delivery.html#sec-governance-compliance-mapping">#sec-governance-compliance-mapping</a>
  </div>

  <div class="ws-instruction">
    With legal or compliance present, mark each framework yes or no and name the products, data types and jurisdictions that bring each yes into scope. For every in-scope framework, record today's posture, the gap, a named owner and the real audit or filing date. Block B is derived from your scope decisions; read it aloud and transcribe its mandatory rows, do not negotiate the floor. On the reverse, record one approved topology per data class from the executed agreement and obtain security, legal and procurement sign-off. Unknown scope is recorded as no, with an owner and date.
  </div>

  <div class="ws-block">
    <p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 1mm">This section provides awareness of regulatory frameworks that intersect with AI-assisted software development. It is not legal advice. Specific requirements vary by jurisdiction, industry, and use case. Consult qualified legal counsel for your organization's compliance obligations. <span class="prior-src">ch05 L181</span></p>
    <p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 2mm">That said, ignorance is not a viable compliance strategy. <span class="prior-src">ch05 L183</span></p>
  </div>

    <p style="font-size:7.4pt;margin:1mm 0 0">Column 7 is assessed against the recommended posture in column 6, not against the framework in general. A scope marked no still needs a named owner and date if the scope is unknown.</p>

  <div class="ws-block">
    <p style="font-size:7.4pt;border-left:1mm solid #566878;padding:1mm 2mm;margin:1mm 0">
      <b>How to read the governance floor.</b> If you are SOC 2-scoped, rows 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 are critical — you will face audit findings if any of these are at "None." If you handle payment data under PCI DSS, rows 1, 2, 3, and 4 are your floor. If you ship to EU markets and your product touches high-risk categories, the EU AI Act makes rows 1, 3, and 6 non-negotiable. Start where your regulatory exposure intersects with your lowest maturity.
      <span class="prior-src">ch05 L94</span>
    </p>

  </div>

  <div class="ws-instruction">
    For each data-classification or repository class you operate, select exactly one topology and state what crosses the network, the approved endpoint and region, the provider's contractual retention terms and the control that authorises this deployment. Obtain separate security, legal and procurement signatures. Record IP ownership and licensing only from your own named counsel; the book does not answer that question.
  </div>

  <div class="ws-block">
    <h2>C — Deployment topology per data class
      <span class="ws-block-note">one row per internal data or repository class; use another copy if you operate more classes</span></h2>

    <table class="ws">
      <colgroup>
        <col style="width:3%"><col style="width:13%"><col style="width:19%"><col style="width:11%">
        <col style="width:12%"><col style="width:16%"><col style="width:14%"><col style="width:12%">

      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th></th>
          <th><span class="fno">15</span> Data class or repository class</th>
          <th><span class="fno">16</span> Topology — choose one</th>
          <th><span class="fno">17</span> What crosses the network</th>
          <th><span class="fno">18</span> Approved model endpoint</th>

          <td class="fill">
            <div class="prior">
              <b>Full local.</b> Client, harness, agent source code, and model all run on the developer's laptop. Ollama or a local GGUF serves inference; the harness reads files from the local checkout. Nothing leaves the machine. Useful for air-gapped work, compliance-sensitive repos, or zero-cost experimentation.<br>
              <b>Hybrid — local client, cloud model.</b> The client, the harness, and the agent source code stay local; only inference calls cross the network. This is the default for most developers running Claude Code or Copilot CLI against a cloud-hosted model. Primitives remain local files; the model never persists them.<br>
              <b>Full cloud.</b> Client, harness, model, and agent source code all run in the cloud. GitHub's Copilot Coding Agent is the canonical example: a pull-request event triggers a cloud-hosted harness that checks out the repo, loads primitives from the commit, drives inference, and pushes commits — all without touching a developer's machine.
              <span class="prior-src">ch11 L65-67</span>
            </div>
